nodes.label: Recommendation: the command does not edit scope rows
nodes.rationale: /scope owns those files (spec 0002), and a second writer would break when their shape changes. Marking inherited rows 'existing' is one step in the written path.

nodes.label: Force: the two apps disagree on their own identity, and the Android ID is not in reverse DNS form
Recommendation: --check accepts two states, foundation and derived
nodes.rationale: One check then runs unchanged in both repositories and catches a half finished derivation in either. A check that passes only after derivation was the runner up and would fail in the foundation itself.

nodes.label: Recommendation: the command refuses to run on a derived checkout
nodes.rationale: A second run would wipe the product's own verification record. A later change of name or ID is an edit of the two identity files.

nodes.label: Force: shared/config/README.md keeps bundle and application IDs in Xcode or Gradle, not in the shared config schema
Recommendation: the identity files stay native
nodes.rationale: shared/config/README.md keeps application IDs in Xcode or Gradle. One shared file read by both builds was the runner up; it would break that rule and tie the two platforms together.

nodes.label: The Linux proof runs on every push; the native proof runs by hand before a foundation tag
nodes.rationale: scripts/test.sh does not read the application ID, so only a native build tests a changed identity, and that cost is paid once per release.

nodes.label: The Linux proof is one unit test, not a second run of scripts/test.sh
nodes.rationale: A cross check showed that a full second run doubles the lint, the tests and a UniFFI compile while proving almost nothing new, since those steps never read the identity. A --self-test form that ran everything in a copy was the runner up.

nodes.label: Force: stable names make a merge clean (31 code and config files and 13 paths carry the foundation name)
Option 2 (rejected): template copy with a full rename and a fresh history
nodes.rationale: Pros: no trace of the foundation name and a clean history. Cons: unrelated histories mean a foundation fix is moved by hand as a patch per product; the rename must rewrite project.pbxproj, the scheme, the validator constants, both generators and the bindings, each of which can break in a way only a native build shows; the script grows with every name the foundation adds.

nodes.label: Recommendation: --check does not look for hosted run links
nodes.rationale: The command writes the record from a template, so the record is right by construction. A link test would depend on the exact spelling of a URL and on a file that /scope rewrites.

nodes.label: The narrow choice comes first: a full rename stays possible later inside one product, the reverse move does not
nodes.rationale: The engineer first chose to rename every name (Option 2), then chose product identity only once the conflict with merging was laid out. Leaving the merge path is reversible in one direction only.

nodes.label: Every native run compares the built app with the identity file
nodes.rationale: The greeting tests never read the ID, so without that comparison a run under the sample identity would pass even if the build ignored the identity file.

nodes.label: No References section
nodes.rationale: Every decision in the spec rests on the repository itself.

nodes.label: One name and one application ID as input
nodes.rationale: The same ID is used on both platforms, with an override per platform for a product that already has different IDs in the stores.

nodes.label: Recommendation: Python under tooling/derive/ with a shell entry in scripts/
nodes.rationale: This is the shape the generators already use: Python 3.9 with the standard library only and no new dependency. A pure shell script was the runner up and lost on input checks and tests.

nodes.label: Recommendation: tags are named foundation-vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
nodes.rationale: The prefix keeps them apart from a product's own release tags in the same clone. A plain v prefix was the runner up.

nodes.label: Recommendation: the origin line records where a product started and never changes
nodes.rationale: Later releases are visible in git log --merges. Rewriting the line on each merge was the runner up and would make the word 'started' untrue.

nodes.label: Force: identity is spread over files the foundation keeps editing (App.xcconfig, Project.xcconfig, project.pbxproj, app/build.gradle.kts, res/values/app.xml)
Recommendation: one identity file per platform that the foundation never edits again
nodes.rationale: Git reports a conflict when two sides change neighbouring lines, and identity lines inside Project.xcconfig or build.gradle.kts sit next to lines the foundation will change. Editing the values in place was the runner up.

nodes.label: Force: a copy inherits claims it never earned (the verification record and the scope index name a hosted run in the foundation repository)
Force: foundation fixes must reach products (a fix typed again in each product will not be applied)
Force: the knowledge graph is tied to this checkout (74 tracked cache files under a path-named folder, one owner specific string)
Force: one maintainer, and real caller first (R8): an unchecked step rests on one person and no tool may exist before something calls it
Force: two copies of the foundation carry the same ID, so one installs over the other
Option 1 (chosen): clone and merge, product identity in two files, one init command
nodes.rationale: Pros: a foundation release reaches a product by git merge with conflicts only where the product changed the same lines; the changing surface is two files so the command and its check stay small; the Xcode project, scheme and build scripts are never rewritten. Cons: foundation names stay visible in product code; a product carries the foundation's commit history; a command and its tests are kept for a job that runs once per product.

nodes.label: Option 3 (rejected): a written checklist, no command
nodes.rationale: Pros: nothing to build, test or keep running, and it fits the rule that a tool needs a caller. Cons: each product is renamed slightly differently and a missed step shows up late; nothing tells a contributor whether a checkout is fully derived; the list goes stale silently when the foundation moves a value.

nodes.label: Without a decision the first product would be renamed by search and replace, differing from the next product in ways nobody chose
Inherited scope rows and specs stay as history
nodes.rationale: The evidence is what gets emptied: the verification record and the hosted run link.

nodes.label: Recommendation: no changelog file and no sync command yet
nodes.rationale: Tags and a path limited git log give the list of changes for one maintainer. Both get built when the first foundation release is merged into a product, which is their real caller.

nodes.label: Only identifiers follow a rename, never prose
nodes.rationale: With product identity only, no document needs rewriting. The one README command that names the ID reads it from the identity file.

nodes.label: Premise: four coupled decisions in one spec (which names change, how a copy is made, what happens to inherited records, how updates arrive)
nodes.rationale: Each decision constrains the others and a split would let them drift. The risk is building update machinery before any product exists, so the spec decides only what cannot be changed cheaply after the first product starts and builds only what the first derivation calls. The first derived product is the real caller ADR 0001 asks for; the command that takes a later foundation release is described, not built.

nodes.label: Recommendation: after derivation the product owns docs/scope/, docs/specs/ and the verification record
nodes.rationale: On a later merge the product keeps its own side of those paths. No rule file links to a numbered row or spec, so nothing dangles. Sharing one numbering sequence with the foundation was the runner up and collides on the first row either side adds.
